config.title: Build versioned APIs v1 and v2 with compatibility

intro.title: Build versioned APIs v1 and v2 with compatibility
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple Node.js API that supports two versions (v1 and v2) of an endpoint, allowing older clients to keep working while new features are added. You will learn how to use Express.js routing to create versioned API paths, such as '/api/v1/data' and '/api/v2/data'. The core concept is API versioning, which helps maintain compatibility as your application evolves. You'll work with basic JavaScript functions, Express middleware, and JSON responses to return different data structures for each version.
intro.usecase: Versioned APIs are essential for maintaining and evolving web services without breaking existing clients. In real-world applications like e-commerce platforms, a v1 API might handle basic product listings and checkout, while a v2 API introduces new features like personalized recommendations or advanced payment methods. This pattern ensures that mobile apps or third-party integrations using the older API continue to function seamlessly, while new features are rolled out in v2. Developers implement this in Node.js to support long-term compatibility, similar to how social media platforms gradually update their APIs to add new data fields or endpoints without disrupting legacy integrations.

objectives: Implement a basic Express server with separate route files for API versions
Configure route handlers to respond with version-specific data structures
Apply middleware to parse JSON request bodies for both API versions
Construct versioned endpoints that maintain backward compatibility
Initialize and test API endpoints using tools like Postman or curl
Manipulate response formats to differentiate between v1 and v2 outputs
Integrate a simple versioning strategy using URL paths (/api/v1/, /api/v2/)

steps.title: Import Express and create the Express app
steps.instruction: Import Express using require() and create an Express application instance. Name the instance 'app'.
steps.hint: Use const app = express() after importing the express module.
steps.seedCode: // Import Express and create the app instance here
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have an Express app instance ready for setting up routes.
successCriteria: Express is imported using require() and an app instance is created.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you've both imported Express and created the app instance.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that you've used require('express') and created an app instance with express().

steps.title: Set up middleware for JSON parsing
steps.instruction: Add the Express JSON parsing middleware to your app using app.use(express.json()).
steps.hint: Call app.use() with express.json() as the argument to enable JSON body parsing for incoming requests.
steps.analogousExample:
// Adding middleware to parse JSON
app.use(express.json());
steps.expectedOutcome: Your Express app will now automatically parse JSON request bodies, making them available in req.body.
successCriteria: app.use(express.json()) is added to configure JSON parsing middleware.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're calling app.use() with express.json() as shown in the example.
steps.feedbackWrong: The JSON parsing middleware wasn't added correctly. Review the example and try again.

steps.title: Create the base route for API v1
steps.instruction: Create a GET route at '/api/v1/hello' that returns a JSON welcome message with a 'message' property set to 'Welcome to API v1!'.
steps.hint: Use app.get() to define a route. The callback should send a JSON response using res.json().
steps.expectedOutcome: The API will have a v1 endpoint that returns a welcome message when accessed via GET.
successCriteria: A GET route is defined at '/api/v1/hello' that returns JSON with a 'message' property containing 'Welcome to API v1!'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure the route path is exactly '/api/v1/hello' and it returns JSON with the correct message property.
steps.feedbackWrong: The route wasn't created correctly. Check that you used app.get() with the correct path and returned JSON with the welcome message.

steps.title: Add a POST endpoint for API v1
steps.instruction: Create a POST route at '/api/v1/users' that accepts JSON and returns a success message with the user data.
steps.hint: Use app.post() to define a POST route. The route handler should accept req and res parameters, and respond with a JSON success message.
steps.expectedOutcome: A POST endpoint at '/api/v1/users' that returns a JSON success message with user data from the request body.
successCriteria: The code includes app.post('/api/v1/users', handler) with a route handler that uses req.body and responds with JSON containing a success message.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your route handler properly accesses req.body and returns a JSON response with a success message.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that you're using app.post() with the correct route path '/api/v1/users' and that your handler returns a JSON response.

steps.title: Create the base route for API v2
steps.instruction: Create a GET route at '/api/v2/hello' that returns a JSON response with an enhanced structure. The response should include a 'message' property with the value 'Hello from API v2!' and a 'version' property with the value '2.0'.
steps.hint: Use app.get() with the path '/api/v2/hello' and send a JSON response containing both message and version properties.
steps.expectedOutcome: A new GET endpoint at '/api/v2/hello' that returns a JSON object with message and version properties.
successCriteria: The route '/api/v2/hello' is defined with app.get() and returns a JSON response containing both 'message' and 'version' properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created a route for API v2, but make sure it returns a JSON object with both 'message' and 'version' properties.
steps.feedbackWrong: The route for API v2 is not correctly implemented. Check that you're using app.get() with the correct path and returning a JSON response with the required properties.

steps.title: Add a POST endpoint for API v2 with new features
steps.instruction: Create a POST route at '/api/v2/users' that includes additional validation and returns enhanced response fields.
steps.hint: Use app.post() with the route path, add validation for the request body, and return a JSON response with more fields than the v1 endpoint.
steps.expectedOutcome: A POST endpoint at '/api/v2/users' is created with validation for required fields and returns a JSON response containing additional fields like 'discount' or 'createdAt'.
successCriteria: The code includes app.post('/api/v2/users', ...) with validation logic and returns a JSON response with at least one new field beyond the v1 endpoint.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created the POST route, but it's missing either the validation or the additional response fields. Check the analogous example for guidance.
steps.feedbackWrong: The POST endpoint for '/api/v2/users' is not correctly implemented. Ensure you use app.post() with the correct path and include both validation and enhanced response.

steps.title: Create a compatibility middleware for v1 requests
steps.instruction: Create a middleware function named compatibilityMiddleware that will intercept v1 requests and adapt them to v2 format. Place it after the JSON middleware but before your route definitions.
steps.hint: Define a function that takes three parameters: req, res, and next. Inside, you can check the request URL and modify the request body if needed.
steps.expectedOutcome: A middleware function named compatibilityMiddleware is defined and ready to be used for request adaptation.
successCriteria: The compatibilityMiddleware function is defined with req, res, and next parameters and includes a call to next() to pass control to the next middleware.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've started the middleware function, but make sure it has all three parameters (req, res, next) and includes a call to next() to continue the request chain.
steps.feedbackWrong: The middleware function isn't properly defined. Remember to create a function named compatibilityMiddleware that takes req, res, and next parameters.

steps.title: Apply the compatibility middleware to v1 routes
steps.instruction: Apply the compatibility middleware to all v1 routes by using app.use() with '/api/v1/*' as the path.
steps.hint: Use app.use('/api/v1/*', compatibilityMiddleware) to apply the middleware only to v1 routes.
steps.analogousExample:
// Apply middleware to specific routes
app.use('/admin/*', adminAuthMiddleware);
steps.expectedOutcome: The compatibility middleware will be applied to all routes starting with /api/v1/.
successCriteria: The compatibility middleware is applied using app.use('/api/v1/*', compatibilityMiddleware).
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're using app.use() with the correct path '/api/v1/*' and the middleware function.
steps.feedbackWrong: The compatibility middleware isn't properly applied to v1 routes. Check the path and middleware function.

steps.title: Add request logging middleware
steps.instruction: Create a middleware function named 'requestLogger' that logs all incoming requests with version information.
steps.hint: Define a function that takes req, res, and next parameters, logs the request method, URL, and API version, then calls next().
steps.expectedOutcome: A middleware function that logs request details will be created and ready to be used.
successCriteria: The 'requestLogger' middleware function is defined and logs request method, URL, and version information.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your middleware logs the request details and calls next().
steps.feedbackWrong: The middleware function isn't defined correctly. Check the function name and parameters.

steps.title: Add error handling middleware
steps.instruction: Create an error handling middleware function that catches errors and sends a consistent JSON response with status 500.
steps.hint: Define a function with parameters (err, req, res, next) that logs the error and sends a JSON response with an error message.
steps.expectedOutcome: An error handling middleware function is created that will catch any unhandled errors in the API routes.
successCriteria: Error handling middleware function is defined with proper parameters and sends a JSON response with status 500.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've started the error handling middleware, but make sure it has all four parameters (err, req, res, next) and sends a JSON response with status 500.
steps.feedbackWrong: The error handling middleware isn't quite right. It should be a function that catches errors and sends a consistent error response.

steps.title: Start the Express server
steps.instruction: Add an app.listen() call at the end of your file to start the Express server on port 3000.
steps.hint: Use app.listen(3000, () => { ... }) to start the server and log a message when it's ready.
steps.expectedOutcome: The server will be configured to listen on port 3000 and log a message when started.
successCriteria: app.listen() is called with port 3000 and includes a callback function that logs a server start message.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added app.listen(), but make sure it includes port 3000 and a callback that logs a message.
steps.feedbackWrong: The server isn't properly started. Add app.listen(3000, () => { console.log('Server running on port 3000'); }) at the end of your file.

steps.title: Test the versioned APIs with different endpoints
steps.instruction: Make test requests to both v1 and v2 endpoints to confirm they return appropriate responses.
steps.hint: You can test the endpoints by making HTTP requests to the running server. For example, use a tool like curl, Postman, or your browser to send GET and POST requests to /api/v1/hello, /api/v1/users, /api/v2/hello, and /api/v2/users.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should be able to successfully send requests to all versioned endpoints and receive appropriate responses, verifying that both API versions work correctly with compatibility.
successCriteria: Test requests are made to both v1 and v2 endpoints, and appropriate responses are received.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've made some test requests, but try to test all endpoints (v1 and v2, both GET and POST) to fully verify the versioned APIs.
steps.feedbackWrong: No test requests were made. You need to test the endpoints to verify that both API versions work correctly with compatibility.
